subject: history
title: Hundred Flowers, Great Leap Forward and Famine
welcome_lead: From short-lived liberalisation to the deadliest famine in human history.
meta_desc: Edexcel A-Level adventure on the Hundred Flowers Campaign 1956, the Great Leap Forward 1958-62 and the famine.
final_note: You can explain why utopian planning produced catastrophe.

concepts.def: Mao's invitation to 'let a hundred flowers bloom' encouraging criticism; followed by the Anti-Rightist crackdown from June 1957.
Purge from 1957 in which an estimated 550,000 intellectuals were labelled rightists and persecuted.
Mao's drive for rapid industrialisation and full collectivisation via People's Communes.
Large rural units of about 5,000 households introduced from August 1958, organising labour, food and welfare communally.
Small village steel furnaces producing poor-quality 'pig iron'; symbol of misallocated effort in 1958-59.
1959-62 famine following the Leap; demographic studies suggest around 30 million excess deaths.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Twentieth CPSU Congress (February 1956) and Hungarian Rising worried Mao. The Hundred Flowers Campaign invited intellectuals to criticise the Party. When criticism turned sharp (Storm of May 1957), Mao reversed course. The Anti-Rightist Campaign from June 1957 silenced critics and consolidated his ideological dominance.

Launched at the Chengdu Conference (March 1958), the Great Leap Forward aimed to overtake Britain in 15 years. People's Communes abolished private plots and household cooking. Backyard furnaces yielded unusable iron. Officials inflated grain returns; state procurement followed false figures. Mao's Lushan Conference (July-August 1959) purged Peng Dehuai for criticising the policy.

The catastrophic harvest fell from a real ~200 million tonnes to 143 million by 1960. Cannibalism and infanticide were recorded; provincial reports were buried. By 1961, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping rolled back the Leap, restoring private plots and reducing commune size. Liu reportedly told Mao the famine was '30% natural, 70% man-made'. The political price would be paid in the Cultural Revolution.
